a: A song of the ascents.
t: "A song of the ascents": what the title means
p: Fifteen psalms (120–134) carry this title. "Ascents" may mean pilgrim journeys, temple steps, or the return from exile.
b: Ma'alot comes from 'alah, "go up." People "go up" to Jerusalem from every direction (122:4), and Ezra 7:9 calls the return from exile "the journey up from Babylon" (hamma'alah). The Mishnah links the fifteen songs to the fifteen steps between two temple courts (Mishnah Middot 2:5; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4). The Greek has "song of the steps" and the Latin canticum graduum, so older Christian books call these the Gradual Psalms. The article ("the ascents") suggests a known collection. Numbering: in Hebrew Bibles these short titles stand inside verse 1, so the verse numbers in 120–137 are the same in Hebrew and English. The Greek and Latin number each psalm one lower (Psalm 120 is their 119). See the chapter page for the views.
r: 121:0; 122:4; Ezra 7:9; Isaiah 30:29; Mishnah Middot 2:5; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4

a: To the LORD I called when trouble came
p: Verse 1 speaks of an answered prayer in the past; verses 2–7 plead as if the trouble is still here.
b: The Hebrew verbs in verse 1 are past: "I called ... he answered me." Some read the whole psalm as a thanksgiving, with verses 2–7 quoting the earlier prayer. Others (Kraus, Allen) take verse 1 as the ground of hope: God answered before, so the singer asks again. A third reading, common in older Jewish and Christian commentary, makes the verbs present, "I call ... and he answers." Either way the first pilgrim song starts far from Jerusalem, in trouble, and ends among people who want war.

a: lips that lie
p: The enemy here does not use swords but lies: slander, false charges, broken promises.
b: The psalm's danger is the tongue. In a village society, a false accusation could cost a person land, family and life (Exodus 23:1; 1 Kings 21:10–13). Jewish interpreters read the psalm as a prayer against informers and slanderers: the Targum turns verse 3 into words to "you badmouther ... you informer," and Rashi hears in it Israel among the nations who accuse it. James 3:5–8 calls the tongue a small fire that sets a forest ablaze, an image close to verse 4.

a: What will he give you, and what more will he add
t: An oath formula turned on the liar
p: The words echo the oath "May God do this to you and more," pointing the punishment back at the lying tongue.
b: Hebrew oaths often ran, "Thus may the LORD do to me, and more besides" (Ruth 1:17), or, to another person, "God do this to you, and more besides" (1 Samuel 3:17). Here the singer asks what God will "give" and "add" to the lying tongue, and verse 4 answers: arrows and burning coals. The liar used words like weapons, and the punishment fits: the arrow and the fire that the tongue sent out (57:4; 64:3) come back on it.
orig: מַה־יִּתֵּן לְךָ וּמַה־יֹּסִיף לָךְ (mah-yitten lekha umah-yosif lakh)

a: coals of broom-wood
p: The broom bush (retem) of the desert made a charcoal known for burning hot and long.
b: Retem is the white broom (Retama raetam), a bush of the Negev and Sinai, the shrub Elijah sat under (1 Kings 19:4). Its roots were burned for charcoal (Job 30:4). A rabbinic tale (Genesis Rabbah 98:19), which Rashi repeats, says broom coals look dead outside while they still burn inside. The verse may describe God's punishment for the liar, or the liar's words themselves: they wound from far away like arrows and keep burning like this charcoal. The Greek has "desert coals."

a: I live as a stranger in Meshech
p: Meshech was in central Anatolia, far to the north; Kedar was a tribe of the north Arabian desert, to the south-east.
b: Meshech is one of Japheth's sons (Genesis 10:2), a people of central Anatolia, far to the north (the Mushki of Assyrian records), remembered as far-off and violent (Ezekiel 32:26; 38:2). Kedar is one of Ishmael's sons (Genesis 25:13), a tribe of the north Arabian desert, to the south-east (Isaiah 21:16–17; Jeremiah 49:28). Since the two lie a thousand miles apart, most scholars read them as figures: "I live among barbarians." The singer lives as a ger, a resident foreigner, among people who do not share God's peace. The Targum makes them "the Asians" and "the Arabs" and reads verse 6 as Edom. The Greek read the letters of Meshech differently; see the variant.
r: Genesis 10:2; Genesis 25:13; Ezekiel 27:13; Ezekiel 38:2; Isaiah 21:16–17; Jeremiah 49:28

a: I am peace itself
p: The Hebrew has no verb: "I, peace." The singer is so set on peace that he can be called by its name.
b: Ani shalom, "I (am) peace," is like 109:4, va'ani tefillah, "and I (am) prayer." Shalom is the keyword of the Songs of Ascents. It comes here in verses 6–7, three times in 122:6–8 (with the near word shalvah, "quiet"), and as the closing blessing in 125:5 and 128:6. The first song ends where the pilgrims start: among people who "are ready for war." The road leads toward Jerusalem, whose name Jewish and Christian readers have long heard as "city of peace" (see 122:6). The Greek adds "they fought me without cause"; see the variant.

a: A song for the ascents.
p: Only this title reads lamma'alot, "for the ascents," instead of hamma'alot, "of the ascents."
b: The difference is one letter. Most scholars see no change of meaning. Jewish tradition found a point in it: Rashi cites the Sifre, "not 'of ascents' but 'for ascents': a song for the One who will make ascents for the righteous in the age to come," and the Targum heads every Song of Ascents "the song that was said on the ascents from the abyss," following the Talmud's story of David and the deep (Bavli Sukkah 53a; see the chapter page of Psalm 120). Psalm 121 is often printed on Jewish amulets for a mother and newborn, from its promise that the guardian never sleeps.

a: I raise my eyes toward the mountains
p: The mountains may be Zion's hills, the place of help, or the dangerous hills the pilgrim must cross.
b: Three readings. (1) The hills are where help lives: Jerusalem stands on "the holy mountains" (87:1), and the pilgrim looks toward the temple. (2) The hills are the danger: robbers and wild animals on the road, or the hilltop shrines of other gods, so the question is sharp, and verse 2 answers, "not from the hills, but from the LORD" (compare Jeremiah 3:23). (3) The pilgrim simply sets out and wonders what lies ahead. The KJV's "from whence cometh my help" read as a statement can sound as if help comes from the hills; the Hebrew me'ayin is a question, "from where?"

a: maker of heaven and earth
t: The maker of heaven and earth
p: This title of God closes three Songs of Ascents and goes back to Melchizedek's blessing of Abraham.
b: "Maker of heaven and earth" comes in 115:15, 121:2, 124:8, 134:3 and 146:6. Its roots are older: Melchizedek blesses Abram by "God Most High, maker of heaven and earth" (Genesis 14:19, 22, using a different verb). For a pilgrim in hostile country, the point is plain: the God of Zion is not a local god of one hill, but the maker of the whole world, including the road. The Apostles' Creed's "maker of heaven and earth" carries the same phrase into Christian worship.

a: May he never let your foot slide
t: A second voice, and a wish
p: "My help" becomes "your foot": someone answers the pilgrim. The Hebrew is a wish, "may he not," not only a promise.
b: From verse 3 on the psalm says "you," not "I." Many think a priest or a family member blesses the traveler at the start of the journey, or the pilgrim speaks to himself. The verbs in verse 3 use the Hebrew negative 'al, which marks a wish or a request ("may he not"), while verse 4 switches to lo', a flat statement ("he does not"). The Plain English Translation keeps the change: the blessing becomes a certainty. A slipping foot is the picture of disaster on a mountain path (38:16; 66:9; 94:18).

a: does not doze and does not sleep
p: Elijah mocked Baal as a god who might be asleep. Israel's guardian never is.
b: On Mount Carmel Elijah taunted the prophets of Baal: "Maybe he's asleep, and he'll wake up" (1 Kings 18:27). In Canaanite myth Baal dies and must be revived. The psalm denies any such weakness in Israel's God. Other psalms cry "Wake up!" to God (44:23; 59:4–5; 78:65), but they describe how things feel, not what God is; this verse says what God is. The word shomer, "guard, keeper," comes six times in the psalm (verses 3, 4, 5, 7 twice, 8): the guardian of Israel is also the guardian of one traveler.

a: The LORD is the shade beside your right hand
p: In a land of hard sun, shade means life. The right hand is where a defender stands in battle or in court.
b: Shade is a picture of protection (91:1; Isaiah 25:4; 32:2), and the "right hand" is where a protector or advocate stands (16:8; 109:31; 110:5). A common explanation is that a soldier's shield covered his left side, so a companion guarded his right. The Targum adds a later Jewish custom: God shades you "because of the mezuzah fixed on the right side of your doorway." Christian readers hear the same promise in Jesus' words about the Father's keeping (John 10:28–29; 17:11–12).

a: or the moon in the night
p: Ancient people believed the moon could harm a sleeper, as the sun could at noon.
b: Sunstroke was a known danger (2 Kings 4:18–20; Isaiah 49:10; Jonah 4:8). Many ancient peoples also blamed the moon for fevers and fits. The Greek word for epilepsy in Matthew 4:24 and 17:15, selēniazomai, means "moonstruck," and English "lunatic" comes from Latin luna, "moon." The Targum says the LORD will keep away the noonday spirits and the night demons (lilin). The psalm does not explain these fears; it says the guardian covers both day and night.
r: 2 Kings 4:18–20; Isaiah 49:10; Jonah 4:8; Matthew 4:24; Matthew 17:15; Revelation 7:16

a: your going out and your coming in
p: A Hebrew way of saying "all you do": leaving home and coming back, starting and finishing.
b: Moses promises Israel, "You will be blessed coming in and blessed going out" (Deuteronomy 28:6), and the phrase covers work, war and daily life (2 Samuel 3:25; 1 Kings 3:7). For a pilgrim it also fits the journey itself, out from home and back again. The Targum spells it out: "your going out to business and your coming in to study Torah." The last line, "from this moment on and for all time," turns one trip into a whole life. Jews and Christians use the verse as a blessing for travelers and for people leaving home.

a: Of David.
p: Four Songs of Ascents name David (122, 124, 131, 133). Many scholars think the name was added later.
b: Read as history, the title makes David the singer who longs for the house his son would build; Rashi and the Midrash have David hear people say, "When will the old man die, so Solomon can build the temple?" Most critical scholars note that the psalm looks back on "thrones that belong to David's house" (122:5) and that pilgrims already stand in Jerusalem's gates, so they date it to a time when the temple stood, often after the exile. The Greek copies differ here; see the variant.

a: Let's go to the LORD's house.
p: The words of neighbors setting out for a feast. The Mishnah records a call like it for the first-fruits procession.
b: Prophets used the same call for Israel's pilgrim feasts: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD" (Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2, fresh rendering), and "Get up, let us go up to Zion, to the LORD our God" (Jeremiah 31:6, fresh rendering). The Mishnah describes villagers gathering in a town square before bringing their first fruits; at dawn the leader would say Jeremiah's words, and a flute played before them all the way to the Temple Mount (Mishnah Bikkurim 3:2–3). Psalm 122 is the joy of hearing that invitation.
r: Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2; Jeremiah 31:6; Zechariah 8:21; Mishnah Bikkurim 3:2

a: Our feet were standing
p: The Hebrew "were standing" can mean "now we stand here" or "we once stood there."
b: The verb hayu 'omdot ("were standing") can describe the moment of arrival ("here we are, standing in your gates!") or a memory told after going home. Some read the whole psalm as sung inside the city at the end of the journey; others as a pilgrim's memory. The Greek has "in your courts," not "gates." Rashi, following the Midrash, reads "our feet stood firm in battle" because Jerusalem's gates were full of Torah study.

a: whose parts are joined into one
p: Close-packed buildings, a united people, or (in Jewish tradition) the heavenly Jerusalem joined to the earthly one.
b: Shechubberah-lah yachdav is literally "which is joined to itself together." (1) A compact city: houses packed inside the walls after rebuilding (Nehemiah 7:4 says it was large but thinly settled, so some date the psalm earlier). (2) A people joined together: the tribes who meet there (122:4) and "brothers" (122:8; 133:1). (3) The Targum and the Talmud read two Jerusalems: "Jerusalem that is built in heaven, like the city joined to it on earth" (Bavli Taanit 5a). Christian readers took up the heavenly city in Galatians 4:26, Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2.

a: the tribes of Yah
p: The Hebrew uses Yah, the short form of God's name, as in "Hallelu-yah."
b: Yah is a short form of the divine name YHWH, found in poetry (68:4; Exodus 15:2) and in "Hallelujah." The Plain English Translation keeps "Yah" wherever it stands alone, as in the site's Exodus 15:2: here, in 130:3 and in 135:4. Inside "hallelu-yah" it stays "Praise the LORD!" (135:1, 3, 21). "The tribes went up" looks back to Israel as twelve tribes, though after 722 BC the northern tribes were gone; the phrase speaks of the whole people of God gathered in one city. Rashi points out that the family names in Numbers 26 ("the Reubenites," Hebrew ha-Re'uveni) are framed by the letters h and y, the letters of Yah, as though God signed his name on every tribe.

a: by a decree given to Israel
p: The Law told every Israelite man to appear before the LORD three times a year, at the three pilgrim feasts.
b: The decree is the pilgrimage law: "Three times a year all your males are to appear before the LORD your God in the place he will choose: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks and at the Feast of Booths" (Deuteronomy 16:16; compare Exodus 23:17; 34:23–24). Women and children came too (1 Samuel 1:3–7; Luke 2:41–44). 'Edut is "decree" in this site's translation (terms.json). Isaiah 30:29 pictures pilgrims singing on the way, and Josephus describes the vast Passover crowds in Jerusalem in his own day (Josephus, Jewish War 6.423–425).
r: Deuteronomy 16:16; Exodus 23:17; Exodus 34:23–24; 1 Samuel 1:3; Luke 2:41–44; Isaiah 30:29

a: thrones were placed for judging
p: Jerusalem was also the seat of the royal court, where the king and his house heard cases.
b: Israel's king was the highest judge (2 Samuel 15:2–4; 1 Kings 3:16–28). Solomon built "the Porch of Judgment" where he would give judgments (1 Kings 7:7). Jehoshaphat set up a court in Jerusalem of priests, Levites and family heads (2 Chronicles 19:8). The plural "thrones" may mean the king with his sons or officials. Pilgrims came both to worship and to seek justice. Jesus promises the Twelve thrones for judging the tribes (Matthew 19:28).

a: Ask for peace for Jerusalem
p: In Hebrew, the verse rings with the sounds of shalom and Yerushalayim: sha'alu shelom Yerushalayim yishlayu.
b: The line plays on the sounds sh, l and m: "sha'alu (ask) shelom (peace) Yerushalayim, yishlayu (may they be at ease)"; then shalom and shalvah ("quiet") in verse 7, and shalom again in verse 8. Jerusalem's old name was Salem (Genesis 14:18; 76:2), and Jews and Christians have long heard "peace" in it, though the name probably meant "foundation of (the god) Shalem." Many Jews and Christians pray this verse today; some apply it to the modern city and state, others to the city of God in a wider sense.
orig: שַׁאֲלוּ שְׁלוֹם יְרוּשָׁלָםִ יִשְׁלָיוּ (sha'alu shelom Yerushalayim yishlayu)

a: I will seek what is good for you.
p: The pilgrim seeks Jerusalem's good; Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the good of Babylon.
b: The verb biqqesh, "seek," is the pilgrim's duty to the city of God. Jeremiah used the same idea in a startling way for the exiles: "Seek the peace of the city I sent you to as exiles, and pray for it to the LORD. When it has peace, you will have peace" (Jeremiah 29:7, fresh rendering). Nehemiah, who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, is described as "seeking the good" of Israel (Nehemiah 2:10). Love for one's own people and city, the psalm says, flows from love for God's house.

a: you whose seat is in the heavens
t: The one who sits in heaven
p: The Hebrew form hayyoshvi has an old poetic ending. God's seat is a throne: he rules from heaven.
b: Yashav, "sit," often means "sit enthroned" (2:4; 29:10; 113:5). The odd ending -i in hayyoshvi is an old poetic form found in a few psalms (113:5–9; 114:8); Rashi calls it an extra letter. The singer, mocked by people at ease on earth (123:4), looks past them to the one ruler who sits above them all. Jesus taught his disciples to pray to "our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9).

a: their master's hand
p: Slaves watched their master's hand for a signal, for food, or for mercy.
b: In a household, the hand of the master or mistress gave orders, handed out food, and held the rod. Slaves watched it for a sign of what to do and of how they would be treated. The Targum makes the point food: slaves look for what is left from the master's table. The psalm's picture is not of fear but of dependence: we can do nothing until he shows us grace. 'Eved means "slave" or "servant" by context; here the picture is of household slaves. The Hebrew "masters" is plural, perhaps a plural of rank.

a: Be gracious to us, LORD, be gracious to us!
p: The Greek here is eleēson hēmas, Kyrie, the prayer the church sings as "Kyrie eleison."
b: Chonnenu, "show us grace," comes from the same root as channun, "gracious" (Exodus 34:6). The Greek Psalter renders it eleēson hēmas, Kyrie, eleēson hēmas, the words of the blind men and the lepers in the Gospels (Matthew 9:27; Luke 17:13) and of the Kyrie in Christian liturgy, East and West. The doubled cry shows how urgent it is.

a: the jeering of the comfortable
p: The mockers are "at ease": people with power and security, perhaps neighbors who sneered at the returned exiles.
b: Sha'anannim, "those at ease," is a word for the secure and careless (Amos 6:1; Isaiah 32:9–11; Zechariah 1:15, where the nations are "at ease" while Jerusalem lies in ruins). Many scholars think of the small Judean community after the exile, mocked by stronger neighbors such as Sanballat and Tobiah when they tried to rebuild (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1–4). The Targum and Rashi speak of "the nations at ease" who scorn Israel. See the variant on "the proud."

a: Of David.
t: "Of David" in the Greek and at Qumran
p: The Hebrew names David in four Songs of Ascents. The Greek copies and the Qumran scroll do not agree on which.
b: The Hebrew titles 122, 124, 131 and 133 "Of David." In Swete's edition, Codex Sinaiticus has the name in all four; Alexandrinus and the Verona and Zurich Psalters lack it in 122 and 124; the Zurich Psalter lacks it in 131; and the first hand of Alexandrinus and the Zurich Psalter lack it in 133. The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a) has "of David" in 122 and 133, and also in 123, which the Hebrew leaves unnamed; its titles for 124 and 131 are lost. For 127 the Verona Psalter adds "of Solomon," where Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have no name (see the variant on 127:0).

a: so let Israel say
t: A leader's line, the people's answer
p: The phrase invites the crowd to repeat the opening line, as in 118:2–4 and 129:1.
b: "Let Israel say" marks a worship leader calling on the congregation to take up the words. The first line is sung, then repeated with the people (124:1–2; 129:1–2). This is how Levite choirs and pilgrim crowds sang (Ezra 3:11; 2 Chronicles 7:3). The Hebrew also has late features, the relative she- ("who") and 'azai ("then"), which many scholars take as signs that the psalm was written or reworked after the exile.

a: then they would have gulped us down alive
p: Enemies are pictured like Sheol, the grave that swallows the living.
b: The image recalls Korah's rebels, swallowed by the ground so that "they go down alive to Sheol" (Numbers 16:30), and the wicked who say, "We'll gulp them down alive, the way Sheol does" (Proverbs 1:12). Jeremiah says Nebuchadnezzar "swallowed me like a sea monster" (Jeremiah 51:34). The psalm moves from beasts (verse 3), to floods (verses 4–5), to teeth (verse 6), to a trap (verse 7): each danger is worse, and each time the LORD was "with us."

a: a torrent would have run up over our necks
p: The word often translated "soul" here means the throat or neck, the place the water rises to.
b: Nefesh first meant "throat," then "breath," "life" and "self." In flood pictures it keeps its physical sense: "the water has reached my throat" (69:1; Jonah 2:5). The KJV's "the stream had gone over our soul" reads as if the soul drowned. The Plain English Translation says "our necks," as the picture requires. In 124:7 the same word means "our life" ("our life got loose").

a: the waters, swollen with pride
p: Zedonim means both "raging" and "arrogant": the flood stands for proud enemies.
b: Zedonim comes from zid, "boil up," used of proud people (19:13; 86:14). In the Psalms and the prophets, floods often stand for nations: Isaiah pictures Assyria as the Euphrates overflowing Judah "up to the neck" (Isaiah 8:7–8). The waters of chaos that God tamed at creation (93:3–4) come back as human pride, and God still holds them back.

a: like torn meat
p: Teref is prey or torn flesh, what a lion or wolf leaves.
b: Teref is the meat a beast of prey tears (Genesis 49:9, 27; Nahum 2:12). The enemies are pictured as wild animals, the people as their meal. The blessing "The LORD be blessed!" (baruch YHWH) answers the danger: the people praise God for what did not happen. The Plain English Translation adds "like" to make clear that the people were not literally eaten.

a: from the bird-catchers' trap
p: Bird-catchers used spring traps and throw-nets; a broken trap lets the bird fly off.
b: Ancient bird-catchers set a pach, a trap with a spring or a falling net, often baited (Amos 3:5; Proverbs 7:23). Egyptian tomb paintings show large clap-nets pulled shut over flocks. The bird does not break free by its own strength: the trap snaps, and it is gone. The repeated verb (nimletah ... nimlatnu, "got loose ... got loose") gives the joy of the escape.

a: Our help is in the name of the LORD
t: A line for the start of worship
p: Christian worship has opened with this verse for centuries, in the Latin office and in Calvin's Geneva.
b: Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini, "Our help is in the name of the Lord," answered by "who made heaven and earth," is a versicle of the Latin daily office, used at Compline and before blessings. When Calvin reformed worship in Geneva, the Sunday service began with this verse (Calvin's Form of Prayers, 1542), and many Reformed churches still open with it as the "votum." In the psalm it sums up the whole song: it was not human strength, but the LORD.

a: are like Mount Zion
p: The psalm compares those who trust God not to soldiers or walls, but to the mountain itself.
b: Zion "will not totter" (46:5): it stands because God is in it. The people who trust him share its steadiness. Isaiah speaks of a stone God lays in Zion, "a tested stone, a precious cornerstone": whoever trusts will not panic (Isaiah 28:16, fresh rendering, quoted in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6).

a: mountains are all around her
p: The old city sits lower than the hills around it: the Mount of Olives to the east is higher than the Temple Mount.
b: Jerusalem was built on two ridges, and the higher hills around it form a ring: the Mount of Olives and Mount Scopus to the east and northeast, the hill south of the Hinnom Valley, and the western ridge. The Mount of Olives rises roughly 80 meters (about 260 feet) above the Temple Mount. A pilgrim coming over those hills saw the city below, held as in a bowl. The psalm makes the landscape a picture: as the hills ring the city, the LORD rings his people.

a: The rod of the wicked
p: Shevet is a stick, a ruler's scepter, and also the word for "tribe" (122:4). Here it is foreign or wicked rule.
b: The "rod of wickedness" is rule by the wicked, perhaps foreign overlords in the land (Isaiah 14:5). The same word means "tribe" in 122:4, as a tribe was a group under one staff. The promise is that such rule will not "stay" (literally "rest," yanuach) on the land God allotted to his people. The "lot" (goral) recalls the dividing of the land by lot under Joshua (Joshua 14:2; Numbers 26:55).

a: turn their hands to wrong
p: If the wicked ruled too long, even good people might give up and do wrong.
b: The verse gives a reason for God's limit on evil rule: so that the righteous are not pushed into doing wrong themselves. Long injustice wears down faith (73:13–15) and tempts people to compromise to survive. Rashi reads it the other way round: God will not let the wicked rule over the righteous, because the righteous are careful not to reach for wrong. Paul says something like the first reading: God does not let his people be tested beyond what they can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13).

a: Peace on Israel!
p: This closing blessing ends 125 and 128. Paul seems to echo it in Galatians 6:16.
b: Shalom 'al-Yisra'el has no verb in Hebrew, like a shout or a greeting. It closes Psalms 125 and 128, and the mosaic floor of an ancient synagogue at Jericho (about the 500s AD) carries the same words. Paul ends Galatians with "May peace and mercy be on all who will walk by this rule, and on the Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16). Whether Paul's "Israel of God" means the Jewish people, Jewish believers, or the church of Jews and Gentiles is debated; see the topic on church and Israel.

a: turned Zion's fortunes back again
p: KJV "turned again the captivity of Zion"; most modern versions "restored the fortunes." The Hebrew allows both.
b: The phrase shuv shevut (here the rare shivat; in 126:4 shevit or shevut) was long read as "bring back the captives," from shavah, "take captive." Many scholars now derive it from shuv, "turn," a set phrase for reversing someone's fate, since it is used of Job, who was never a captive (Job 42:10). The site renders it "turned ... fortunes back" (85:1), and "brings his people back from captivity" where exile is clearly in view (14:7). Here both fit: the return from Babylon was the great turning of Zion's fortunes.
orig: בְּשׁוּב יְהוָה אֶת־שִׁיבַת צִיּוֹן (beshuv YHWH et-shivat Tsiyyon)

a: we were like people dreaming
p: The Hebrew says "like dreamers." The Greek has "like those comforted," perhaps from another sense of the same root.
b: Cholmim normally means "dreamers": the return was too good to believe. A second Hebrew root chalam means "be healthy, strong" (Job 39:4; Isaiah 38:16), and some scholars read "we were like people made well." The Greek has hōs parakeklēmenoi, "like those comforted", and the Gallican Latin sicut consolati; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew has quasi somniantes, "as if dreaming." The Talmud tells of Honi the circle-drawer, who puzzled over this verse and slept for seventy years (Bavli Taanit 23a).

a: Our mouths overflowed with laughter then
p: Verses 1–3 may look back on a return that has happened, or forward to one hoped for.
b: Most translations read verses 1–3 as past (the return of 538 BC under Cyrus, Ezra 1) and verses 4–6 as a prayer for the hard years after, when the returned community was small and poor (Haggai 1:6–11). Others read the whole psalm as future, "When the LORD restores Zion, we will be like dreamers," since Hebrew verbs of this kind can speak of what is certain to come. Jewish tradition sings it before the grace after meals on Sabbaths and feasts as a song of the future redemption.

a: The LORD has done something great with them.
p: Even outsiders say it. Joel and Mary's song use the same words.
b: Higdil YHWH la'asot, "the LORD has made great to do," is the language of Joel 2:20–21 ("the LORD has done great things") and stands behind Mary's "the Mighty One has worked great things for me" (Luke 1:49). In verse 3 the people take up the nations' words as their own: "The LORD has done something great with us." The return from exile was meant to be a sign to the world (Isaiah 52:10; Ezekiel 36:36).

a: like the stream beds in the Negev
p: The Negev's stream beds lie dry most of the year, then fill suddenly when winter rain falls on the hills.
b: The Negev is the dry south of Judah. Its 'afiqim, "channels," are wadis: bare gullies that can run with flash floods within hours of rain, and then turn green. The prayer asks for a sudden, total change, not a slow recovery. The Talmud, commenting on another verse, says the day of rain is as great as the resurrection of the dead (Bavli Taanit 7a). Rashi reads it as a farmer's hope: dry fields watered by channels after a sowing in tears (126:5).

a: Whoever sows with tears
p: Some scholars link the line to old sowing rites with mourning; most read it as a proverb of hope.
b: Several ancient peoples wept at sowing. In Ugaritic myth, Anat cuts down Mot (Death) like grain and sows him in the field, and the rains return with Baal; some scholars (Mowinckel among them) suggested Israel's farmers knew similar customs. Others see only a farmer's proverb: sowing in a dry year was costly and uncertain, and the harvest came as a gift. The verdict: there is no clear sign that the psalm borrows a ritual; it uses the farmer's year as a picture of exile and return. Jesus says, "Blessed are those who weep now, because you will laugh" (Luke 6:21).

a: carrying the seed bag
p: The phrase may be "the bag of seed," "a handful of seed to scatter," or (KJV) "precious seed."
b: Meshekh comes from mashakh, "draw, drag": a sack drawn on the shoulder, the seed drawn out in handfuls, or the "trail" of seed along the furrow. Amos 9:13 speaks of the one who "draws the seed" (moshekh hazzara'). The KJV's "precious seed" follows a medieval Jewish guess from the sense "price" in Job 28:18. The Hebrew uses doubled verbs ("he goes and goes ... he will come, yes, come"), and the Plain English Translation keeps them.

a: carrying the seed bag
t: Claude's theory: from Meshech to the seed bag
p: The rare word meshekh appears in the first and seventh Songs of Ascents. It may be a deliberate echo.
b: This is my own suggestion. The first Song of Ascents laments "I live as a stranger in Meshech" (120:5), and the Greek and Latin read that word as "my exile has dragged on." Psalm 126 uses the same letters, meshekh, for the bag of seed carried out in tears. If the collectors noticed the sound, the far-off land of 120 becomes the seed of 126: the long exile is the sowing, and the return is the harvest. I know of no commentary that makes this exact link, though the theme of exile as sowing is old (Hosea 2:23; Zechariah 10:9).

a: Of Solomon.
p: Solomon built the temple, the palace and the city, and his birth name was Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD."
b: The title links the psalm to Solomon, who built "the house" (1 Kings 6), and whose name at birth was Jedidiah (2 Samuel 12:25), close to yedido, "his beloved," in verse 2. Rashi says David spoke this psalm about his son. Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have no name in the title, though the Verona Psalter and the Latin have it; see the variant. Critical scholars see a wisdom saying, like Proverbs (also linked to Solomon), placed at the center of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, with seven songs on either side.

a: If the LORD does not build a house
p: A "house" in Hebrew can be a building, a temple, a palace, or a family line. The psalm plays on all of them.
b: God told David that David would not build God a house; God would build David a "house," a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:5, 11–13). The elders blessed Ruth to be like Rachel and Leah, "who built the house of Israel" (Ruth 4:11). Building a house and having sons belong together in Hebrew: bonim, "builders," and banim, "sons" (127:3), sound almost the same. The first half of the psalm is about work, the second about children, and the word play joins them.

a: eating bread earned with pain
p: The word 'atsavim recalls the curse on Adam: "In pain you will eat its yield."
b: 'Atsavim, "pains, toil," is the root of 'itstsavon in Genesis 3:17: "In pain you will eat its yield / all the days of your life." Restless overwork, the psalm says, is life still under the curse. It does not praise laziness (Proverbs 6:6–11) but anxious labor that forgets God. Jesus says the same about worry: the Father feeds the birds, who neither sow nor reap (Matthew 6:25–34).

a: Just so, he gives the one he loves sleep.
t: Sleep as a gift, or a gift in sleep?
p: The line may mean God gives sleep to those he loves, or gives them what they need while they sleep.
b: Hebrew ken yitten lididó shena' can be read as (1) "so he gives his beloved sleep": rest is God's gift, not a waste of time; or (2) "so he gives to his beloved in sleep": God provides while they rest, as the seed grows "night and day" while the farmer sleeps (Mark 4:26–29). Ken may mean "so, likewise" or "surely." Shena' is spelled the Aramaic way. Rashi read shena' as "one who drives away sleep" to study Torah. Yedid, "beloved," echoes Jedidiah, Solomon's name (see 127:0).
orig: כֵּן יִתֵּן לִידִידוֹ שֵׁנָא (ken yitten lididó shena')

a: sons are an inheritance the LORD gives
p: Banim means "sons," and often "children." The psalm calls them an inheritance and wages from God.
b: Nachalah, "inheritance," is the word for Israel's land; sakhar, "wages, reward," is pay for work. Children are both: a gift held in trust and a blessing. In a farming society, sons worked the land and cared for parents in old age. The psalm speaks of God's blessing, not of anyone's worth: Hannah's grief (1 Samuel 1) and God's promise to the childless (Isaiah 56:3–5) show that the Bible does not treat the childless as cursed. Rashi read the "sons" as disciples a teacher raises.

a: like arrows in the hand of a fighter
p: Grown sons were a family's defense and its standing in the town.
b: "Sons of youth" are sons born while the father is young, so they are grown and strong when he is old. Like arrows they protect the household and reach further than the father could alone. The Greek read "sons of the shaken-out," perhaps of exiles driven out. The picture is from a world where family meant security; the next verse moves the scene to the law court.

a: who has filled his quiver full of them
p: Some read this as a call to have as many children as God sends; most as a picture of blessing, not a rule.
b: Since the 1980s, a movement among some conservative Protestants (often called "Quiverfull," from this verse) has taught that couples should not use birth control but should welcome as many children as God gives. Most Jewish and Christian readers take the verse as praise of children as a blessing, not as a rule about family size. The Catholic Church teaches that marriage should be open to life, while allowing couples to space births for serious reasons by natural means. See the box on the chapter page.

a: when they argue with enemies in the gate
p: The gate was the town's court, market and meeting place. A man with grown sons could not be pushed around there.
b: Elders sat at the gate to settle cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–11; Amos 5:12, 15). A man with several grown sons had witnesses and supporters there. "They will not be put to shame" may mean the father and sons together win their case. Rashi applies it to Torah scholars, who argue like enemies over the law and remain friends.

a: Happy is each one who fears the LORD
p: The Hebrew kol, "every," widens the blessing. Rashi says it includes women.
b: Psalm 128 is a wisdom psalm, close to Proverbs: "fearing the LORD" (Proverbs 1:7) means a life of reverent obedience, "walking in his ways." Psalm 1:1 and 112:1 say "Happy is the man"; here it is "Happy is each one." Rashi notes the change and says kol, "every," was put in to include women. The psalm then speaks to a man about his wife and children, but its opening blessing is for anyone.

a: What your own hands have toiled for, you will eat.
p: To eat what you have worked for was the covenant blessing; to see enemies eat it was the curse.
b: The curses of the covenant warn that others will take what Israel works for: "A people you have never known will eat what your soil grows" (Deuteronomy 28:33; compare Leviticus 26:16; Amos 5:11). The prophets promised the reverse: "They will plant vineyards and eat what they bear" (Isaiah 65:21–22, fresh rendering). Psalm 128 answers Psalm 127: work is not "for nothing" when it is done in the fear of the LORD.

a: deep inside your house
p: Yarkete beitekha means the innermost parts of the house, the family's private rooms.
b: In an Israelite house the back rooms were the family's private space, away from the courtyard and the street. The vine is a picture of fruitfulness and also of joy, since wine "makes people glad at heart" (104:15). The Hebrew sets wife and children in verbless lines, like a picture: "Your wife, a fruitful vine ... your children, olive plants." Rashi reads "inner rooms" as a sign of modesty.

a: young olive plants
p: Young olive trees sprout around the trunk of an old one. An olive tree can live for centuries.
b: Shetilim, "plants, shoots," are the saplings that grow up around an olive tree. Olives are slow to bear but live for hundreds of years, and their oil was food, light and medicine. The picture is of a family that goes on for generations, gathered around one table. Jeremiah calls Israel "a green olive tree" (Jeremiah 11:16), and Paul uses the olive tree for God's people (Romans 11:17–24).

a: May the LORD bless you from Zion
p: The priests' blessing goes out from the temple to the pilgrim's home.
b: The words recall the priestly blessing, "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24), and return in 134:3. Pilgrims came up to Zion and went home with a blessing for their household. The blessing reaches "the good of Jerusalem": a family's welfare is tied to the city's. Catholic and other Christian wedding services often use Psalm 128 as the psalm of the rite.

a: And may you see children born to your children.
p: To live to see grandchildren was the picture of a full life.
b: Joseph saw his great-grandchildren (Genesis 50:23); Job saw four generations (Job 42:16). "Children's children are the crown old people wear" (Proverbs 17:6). The psalm moves outward: the man, his wife, his children, his grandchildren, Jerusalem, all Israel. Rashi adds a legal point: with sons and grandsons, no widow will need a brother-in-law marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5), and there will be peace.

a: since I was young
p: Israel speaks as one person, whose "youth" was the time in Egypt.
b: The prophets speak of Israel's youth: "When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son" (Hosea 11:1, fresh rendering; compare Jeremiah 2:2; Ezekiel 23:3). The "I" of Psalm 129 is the nation, attacked from Egypt to Babylon. Jewish readers have prayed it through every later persecution. The Midrash on Psalms compares Israel to a borrowed heifer plowed by ten sons, until its owner cuts the ropes.

a: Across my back the plowmen plowed
p: The image is of whipping: long welts across the back like furrows in a field.
b: Isaiah uses the same picture for Jerusalem under its conquerors: "you laid your back flat like the ground, like a road for travelers to walk on" (Isaiah 51:23, fresh rendering). Micah warned that Zion would be "plowed like a field" (Micah 3:12). Christian readers since the church fathers have heard Christ's scourging (Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 27:26), and Augustine read the psalm as the voice of the whole church. The Greek reads quite differently here; see the variant.

a: he has cut through the ropes of the wicked
p: 'Avot are ropes or cords, here the harness that ties the ox to the plow.
b: The picture continues from verse 3: Israel is the ox, the enemies the plowmen. When God cuts the ropes of the harness, the plowing stops. "Ropes" are also used of bonds and oppression (2:3; Isaiah 5:18; Hosea 11:4). God is "in the right" (tsaddiq): he acts as a just judge, not by chance. The Greek has "the necks of sinners."

a: Let them be shamed and driven back
p: Verses 5–8 ask God to shame Zion's enemies. The curse is mild beside Psalm 137, but it is a curse.
b: The second half turns from thanks to a prayer against "all who hate Zion." It asks for shame and failure, not death: let them be like grass that never ripens and never receives the harvest blessing. Readers have taken it in different ways: a prayer against God's enemies (since hating Zion means hating the city God chose), a wish that oppression come to nothing, or a human cry left in Scripture for honesty. See the topic on the curse psalms and the chapter page of Psalm 137.

a: that dries out before it can be pulled
p: Flat roofs of packed earth sprouted grass after rain, but it had no depth of soil and soon dried up.
b: Houses in Israel had flat roofs of beams, brush and rolled clay. After winter rain, seeds sprouted on them, and in the first hot wind they withered (2 Kings 19:26; Isaiah 37:27). The verb shalaf is uncertain: "draw out" (as a sword), so "before it is pulled up" (Rashi, the Greek), or "before it shoots up" (so many modern versions). Either way, such grass never becomes a harvest. Jesus' parable of seed on rocky ground uses the same idea (Mark 4:5–6).

a: "The LORD's blessing on you!"
p: Harvesters blessed one another in the LORD's name, as Boaz and his workers did in Ruth 2:4.
b: Boaz greeted his harvesters, "The LORD be with you!" and they answered him, "The LORD bless you!" (Ruth 2:4). Psalm 129 imagines Zion's haters as a field so poor that no one passing will speak that blessing. Withholding the blessing is a quiet curse. The words "The Lord be with you" became one of the oldest greetings in Christian worship, answered "And with your spirit."

a: From the depths I have called you, LORD.
p: The Latin first words, De profundis, became the psalm's name. The "depths" are deep waters.
b: Ma'amaqqim, "depths," is used of the deep sea (69:2, 69:14; Isaiah 51:10; Ezekiel 27:34): the speaker is drowning in trouble, guilt, or both. Jonah prays from the same place (Jonah 2:2–3). The Vulgate begins De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine, and the psalm has been known by those words in Western Christianity ever since. On the Talmud's story of David and the deep, see the chapter page of Psalm 120.

a: From the depths I have called you, LORD.
p: Psalm 130 is one of the church's seven Penitential Psalms, and the Catholic Church prays it for the dead.
b: From at least the 500s (Cassiodorus), Western Christians grouped seven psalms as the Penitential Psalms: 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. Psalm 130 is the sixth. In the Catholic Office of the Dead and at funerals the De profundis is prayed for the departed, and it was long said for the souls in purgatory. Protestants kept it as a psalm of forgiveness: Luther set it as the hymn "Aus tiefer Not" (1524). Jews say it in the Ten Days of Repentance between the New Year and the Day of Atonement.

a: Lord, listen to my voice.
p: The psalm alternates the name YHWH ("LORD") with Adonai ("Lord"), a title meaning "my Master."
b: Verses 1–3 and 5–7 move back and forth: YHWH in 130:1, Adonai in 130:2, both in 130:3 (Yah, the short form, then Adonai), YHWH in 130:5, Adonai in 130:6, YHWH in 130:7. Small capitals "LORD" stand for the name; "Lord" for the title. Many Hebrew manuscripts read YHWH in some of the Adonai places, as scribes often swapped the two. The pairing is the language of a servant speaking to the one he belongs to.

a: If you were to keep watch over guilt
p: Shamar 'avonot: to guard or watch over guilt, as a keeper holds a record.
b: Shamar, "watch, keep," is the word for watchmen (127:1; 130:6). Here God is pictured as one who could keep guilt on file, watching for every fault. 'Avon, "guilt," covers both the wrong done and the burden it leaves (32:5; 51:2). The answer is a question: "who would remain standing?" No one could stand in court (1:5; 143:2). Paul makes the same point from Psalm 143:2 in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16.

a: Yet forgiveness is found with you
p: Selichah, "forgiveness," is a word used only of God's pardon. The Greek and Latin read quite differently.
b: The noun selichah appears only here, Nehemiah 9:17 and Daniel 9:9, and the verb salach always has God as its subject: only God forgives in this sense. The Greek has hilasmos, "atonement, propitiation," the word of 1 John 2:2 and 4:10. Jewish liturgy names its prayers for forgiveness Selichot. On the Greek and Latin readings of what follows, see the variant.

a: so that people will stand in awe of you
p: The verse links forgiveness with fear. Readers have long asked why mercy should lead to awe.
b: One might expect forgiveness to remove fear. The psalm says the reverse: because God forgives, people will fear him, that is, honor and obey him rather than despair. Calvin wrote that without hope of pardon, people flee from God; the promise of pardon draws them to worship. Rashi: God gave no agent the power to forgive (Exodus 23:21), so that people fear him and rely on no one else's pardon. Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew has cum terribilis sis; the Greek and the Gallican Latin read "for your name" or "for your law" (see the variant).

a: more than the watchmen look for the morning
p: Night guards on city walls and in the temple waited for daybreak to end their watch.
b: The night was split into watches (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19). For the guard on the wall, dawn meant safety and rest. In the temple, priests and Levites kept watch through the night (134:1), and the morning sacrifice could begin only when a lookout called that the sky was light as far as Hebron (Mishnah Tamid 3:2). The repeated line, "the watchmen for the morning," lets the reader feel the long wait. The Greek and Latin join the line to the next: "from the morning watch until night."

a: For loyal love is with the LORD
p: Two gifts are "with" the LORD: loyal love and redemption.
b: The psalm turns from the speaker to all Israel. Hesed, "loyal love," is God's covenant faithfulness (see 136:1). Pedut, "redemption," comes from padah, "ransom, buy free," used of firstborn sons and of Israel freed from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8). "With him in plenty" (harbeh) promises more than enough. The verse moves from "forgiveness is with you" (130:4) to "loyal love is with the LORD."

a: from all its guilty deeds
t: He will save his people from their sins
p: The last line is echoed in the angel's words about Jesus in Matthew 1:21.
b: Israel expected God to redeem it from enemies and exile. This psalm says he will redeem Israel from its own 'avonot, "guilty deeds," which is the deeper slavery. The angel tells Joseph to name Mary's son Jesus, "for he is the one who will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21), and Titus 2:14 echoes the Greek of this verse: Christ gave himself "to redeem us from all lawlessness" (fresh rendering). Jewish readers hear the promise of the final redemption (Isaiah 59:20).

a: my heart has not grown tall
p: In Hebrew a proud heart is a heart that is "high." The psalm denies it.
b: Gavah lev, "to be high of heart," is the language of pride (Proverbs 16:5; 2 Chronicles 26:16; Ezekiel 28:2). "Eyes that climb high" are haughty looks (18:27; 101:5; Proverbs 6:17). "Great things" and "wonders" (nifla'ot) are often God's own deeds (136:4): the speaker does not try to grasp what belongs to God (Job 42:3). Rashi hears David contrasting himself with Solomon, who made "great things": buildings, gardens and pleasures (Ecclesiastes 2:4–8).

a: like a weaned child lying on its mother
p: A weaned child no longer cries for the breast but rests on its mother. The image is of contentment, not hunger.
b: Israelite children were weaned late, at two or three years (1 Samuel 1:22–24; 2 Maccabees 7:27). A weaned child is no longer restless for milk; it can lie quietly on its mother simply to be near her. The speaker has "leveled" and "hushed" the soul in the same way: no longer demanding, but trusting. The picture of God as a mother appears also in Isaiah 49:15 and 66:13. Some scholars think the speaker is a woman, since she speaks of "my soul" lying on her like the child she carries.

a: Instead I have leveled my soul and hushed it
p: The Hebrew opens with "If I have not," the form of an oath. The Greek read it as a curse on oneself.
b: 'Im lo', literally "if not," is the Hebrew way of swearing "surely I have." The Plain English Translation renders it "Instead," with the sense of a firm claim. The Greek and the Gallican Latin read the verse as a full oath with its curse: "If I was not humble-minded, but lifted up my soul, like a weaned child on its mother, so you would repay my soul" (see the variant). Shiwwiti, "I leveled," is used of smoothing a plowed field (Isaiah 28:25).
orig: אִם־לֹא שִׁוִּיתִי וְדוֹמַמְתִּי נַפְשִׁי ('im-lo' shiwwiti vedomamti nafshi)

a: Israel, wait in hope for the LORD
t: From one soul to all Israel
p: The last line repeats 130:7 almost word for word, joining the two psalms.
b: A quiet personal psalm ends with a call to the whole people, as in 130:7. The collectors seem to have set 130 and 131 side by side as a pair: a cry from the depths, and a soul at rest. "From this moment on and for all time" also comes in 113:2, 115:18, 121:8 and 125:2.

a: all the pain he took on himself
p: 'Unnoto is "his being afflicted" or "his humbling himself." The Greek and Latin read "his meekness."
b: 'Unnoto comes from 'anah, "be bowed down, afflicted." It may mean all David suffered (1 Chronicles 22:14, "in my hard times I have laid up" for the temple), or the hardship he chose: the oath not to rest (132:3–5). The Greek has praütētos, "meekness," and the Gallican Latin mansuetudinis, reading the same consonants as 'anvah, "humility"; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew has adflictionis. "Remember for David" asks God to count David's devotion in favor of his house.

a: I will not set foot in the tent of my house
p: The historical books do not record this oath, though they tell of David's wish to build the LORD a house.
b: In 2 Samuel 7:2 David says, "I live in a house made of cedar, and God's ark lives inside curtains." The psalm turns that wish into a solemn vow not to rest until the ark has a home. Royal vows like this are known from the ancient Near East: kings swore to build or restore a god's temple before enjoying their own palace. "Tent" is old poetic language for a home (Joshua 22:4; 1 Kings 8:66).

a: in Ephrathah we heard about it
t: Ephrathah and the fields of Jaar
p: The verse traces the search for the ark, which stayed at Kiriath-jearim ("town of woods") for twenty years.
b: After the Philistines sent the ark back, it rested at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years (1 Samuel 7:1–2), until David brought it up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6; 1 Chronicles 13). Sedei ya'ar, "fields of the forest," is a short poetic form of that town's name. Ephrathah is the clan region of Bethlehem (Ruth 4:11; Micah 5:2), David's home; 1 Chronicles 2:50 links Ephrathah to the founder of Kiriath-jearim. So "we heard of it" back home; "we found it" in the woods. "It" is feminine in the Hebrew, perhaps meaning the place or the ark.
r: 1 Samuel 7:1–2; 2 Samuel 6:2; 1 Chronicles 13:5–6; 1 Chronicles 2:50; Ruth 4:11; Micah 5:2

a: let us bow low at the footstool for his feet
p: The ark was pictured as the footstool of God, who sat invisible above the cherubim.
b: In the ancient world a king's throne often had a footstool. Israel pictured the LORD enthroned above the cherubim (80:1; 99:1), with the ark beneath as his footstool (99:5; 1 Chronicles 28:2; Lamentations 2:1). To bow at the footstool is to worship at the ark itself. Isaiah widens the picture: "The heavens are my throne and the earth is the stool for my feet" (Isaiah 66:1, fresh rendering).

a: Up, LORD, to your place of rest
p: The cry recalls Moses' words whenever the ark set out, and Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication.
b: "Rise up, LORD!" was Moses' cry each time the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35). Solomon ends his dedication prayer with almost the words of 132:8–10 (2 Chronicles 6:41–42); see the chapter page for the two set side by side. Menuchah, "place of rest," is the place where the ark, and God's people, come to rest at last (Deuteronomy 12:9; 1 Chronicles 28:2; 95:11). Psalm 132 may have been sung when the ark was carried in procession to the temple.

a: May your priests wear righteousness like clothes
p: In 132:16 God answers with something more: the priests will wear salvation.
b: Verse 9 asks that the priests be dressed in tsedeq, "righteousness"; verse 16 answers that they will be dressed in yesha', "salvation." 2 Chronicles 6:41 already has "salvation" in the prayer. The image of clothing for a moral quality is common (Job 29:14; Isaiah 61:10; Revelation 19:8). The faithful (chasidim) who "shout for joy" in 132:9 will "shout and shout for joy" in 132:16: the answer outdoes the prayer.

a: do not turn your anointed one away
p: Hebrew says "do not turn back the face of your anointed one": do not refuse his request.
b: To "turn back someone's face" is to send him away with his request denied (1 Kings 2:16–20). The "anointed one" (meshiach) is the reigning king of David's line, perhaps praying at the festival. Later readers heard the coming Messiah. In 2 Chronicles 6:42 the standard Hebrew text (the Leningrad codex) has the plural, "your anointed ones"; see the chapter page.

a: The LORD swore to David in truth
p: David swore to the LORD (132:2); now the LORD swears to David. The psalm is built on the two oaths.
b: The second half answers the first: David vowed a house for God; God vows a "house," a dynasty, for David (2 Samuel 7:11–16; Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 89:35). Peter quotes this verse at Pentecost: David knew "that God had sworn with an oath to him to seat one of his descendants on his throne," and so spoke of Christ's resurrection (Acts 2:30, fresh rendering). "The fruit of your body" echoes the language of Luke 1:42.

a: If your sons keep my covenant
p: Here the promise has a condition. In 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 89 it is unconditional. Readers have weighed the two.
b: 2 Samuel 7:14–15 and Psalm 89:30–37 say God will punish David's sons who sin but will never take away his loyal love. Psalm 132:12 says the throne passes on if the sons keep the covenant (compare 1 Kings 2:4; 9:4–7). Some scholars think the conditional form is older; others think it was shaped after the exile, when the line had lost the throne. Many Jewish and Christian readers hold both: individual kings could forfeit the throne, but God would keep his promise to David's line. Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus (Luke 1:32–33).

a: Zion is the place the LORD has chosen
p: God's choice of David and of Zion are joined, as in 78:68–70.
b: Deuteronomy speaks of "the place the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5) without naming it. The psalm names it: Zion. Psalm 78:68–70 sets the same pair side by side: "He chose Judah's tribe instead, / Mount Zion, the one he loved ... Then he chose his servant David." Ivvah, "longed for," is a strong word of desire.

a: Her food I will surely bless
p: The Hebrew says "her provision"; some Greek copies and the Gallican Latin read "her widow."
b: Tsedah, "provision, food for a journey" (Genesis 42:25; Joshua 9:11), is spelled here tseydah, a form that also means "game, hunting" (Genesis 27:3); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew has venationem, "hunting." Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) and Alexandrinus read chēran, "widow", and the Gallican Latin has viduam; a corrector of Sinaiticus and the Zurich Psalter have thēran, "game," which matches the Hebrew and differs by one letter. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; see the variant.

a: There I will make a horn spring up for David
p: A horn stands for strength; a lamp for the life of a family that has not been snuffed out.
b: The "horn" is the strength of a wild ox, a picture of a king's power (89:17, 89:24; 1 Samuel 2:10). "Spring up" uses tsamach, "sprout," the root of tsemach, "Branch," a name for the coming king (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). The "lamp" recalls God's promise that "a lamp will burn for David" (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4). Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, says, "In the house of David his servant / he has raised up for us a horn of salvation" (Luke 1:69).

a: but his crown will gleam on him
p: Yatsits, "gleam," comes from tsits, a flower and also the gold plate on the high priest's turban.
b: Tsits means a blossom (Isaiah 40:7) and the shining gold plate on the high priest's headdress, engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36). Nezer, "crown," is the royal diadem (2 Samuel 1:10) and also the consecration of a Nazirite or priest. So the king's crown will "flower" and "gleam." The Greek reads "on him my holiness will flower", taking nezer as consecration.

a: when brothers live together, all as one
p: The words may describe a family keeping its land undivided, or all Israel gathered at the feast.
b: Deuteronomy 25:5 uses the same words, "when brothers live together," for brothers who share their father's land without dividing it. The psalm may be a family proverb applied to the whole nation, gathered at Zion from north and south. The Talmud and later Jewish readers applied it to scholars at study. Augustine said the verse gave birth to monasteries, where brothers live as one. The song is widely sung in modern Hebrew as "Hinneh mah tov."

a: Aaron's beard
p: Moses poured the anointing oil on Aaron's head (Leviticus 8:12). Oil running down pictures blessing that spreads.
b: The holy anointing oil, made with myrrh, cinnamon and other spices (Exodus 30:22–33), was poured so freely on Aaron that it ran down his beard. "Flows down" (yored) is said three times in the psalm: of the oil twice and of the dew once. The blessing comes down from above, like the oil from the head to the robes, and from Hermon to Zion. Some read "the neck of his robes" as the opening of the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:32), others the hem.

a: like Hermon's dew coming down
p: Mount Hermon, far to the north, is famous for heavy dew. Its dew cannot literally fall on Zion. The line is a picture.
b: Hermon (about 2,800 m, 9,200 ft) is snow-capped much of the year, and its slopes are drenched by night dew. Zion is about 200 km (125 miles) to the south, and its summers are dry. The picture is of the rich dew of the north falling on Jerusalem: unity among the tribes is as reviving as dew in a dry land. Dew stands for God's blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5).

a: There is where the LORD has ordered the blessing
p: God "commands" the blessing: he orders it to come, as in Leviticus 25:21 and Deuteronomy 28:8.
b: Tsivvah, "command," is used of blessing in Leviticus 25:21 ("I will order my blessing for you") and Deuteronomy 28:8. "There" may be Zion or the place where brothers live as one. "Life for all time" (chayyim 'ad-ha'olam) may mean long life or life without end; Daniel 12:2 uses "life for all time" of the resurrection. The Targum reads it the same way: "there the LORD ordered the blessing."

a: who stand in the LORD's house night after night
t: The night watch in the temple
p: Priests and Levites kept watch in the temple through the night. The last Song of Ascents speaks to them.
b: The Mishnah describes priests guarding the temple at night in three places and Levites in twenty-one (Mishnah Middot 1:1), and Levite singers who served "day and night" (1 Chronicles 9:33). The psalm may be a closing exchange at the feast: pilgrims about to go home call on the night staff to bless the LORD (134:1–2), and the priests answer with a blessing on the pilgrims (134:3). The Targum adds that they stand "and praise in the nights."

a: Raise your hands toward the sanctuary
p: Lifting the hands, palms open, was the ancient posture of prayer and praise.
b: Many Near Eastern images show worshipers standing with hands raised. In Israel too (28:2; 63:4; 141:2; 1 Kings 8:22; Lamentations 2:19), hands were raised "toward the sanctuary" (qodesh), the holy place. Paul asks that people pray "lifting holy hands" (1 Timothy 2:8, fresh rendering), and the posture is still used in many churches.

a: May the LORD bless you from Zion
p: Psalm 134 has long been the psalm of the church's last service of the day.
b: Benedict's Rule appoints Psalms 4, 91 and 134 for Compline every night (Rule of Benedict 18), and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours still uses Psalm 134 at Compline. It ends the Songs of Ascents: the pilgrim who set out living next to "one who hates peace" (120:6) ends in the temple, blessed from Zion. The last line joins the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24) to the confession "maker of heaven and earth" (121:2; 124:8).

a: Praise, you servants of the LORD
p: Psalm 135 is built almost entirely of lines found elsewhere in Scripture.
b: Verse 1 echoes 113:1 and verse 2 134:1; verse 4 echoes Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6; verse 5 Exodus 18:11; verse 7 Jeremiah 10:13; verses 10–12 recall 136:17–22; verse 13 Exodus 3:15; verse 14 Deuteronomy 32:36; verses 15–20 Psalm 115:4–11. Such a mosaic is not a lack of skill but a way of praising with the words Israel already knew. Some scholars think it was composed for worship after the exile.

a: Make music to his name, because that is a delight
t: Lovely: the name, or the music?
p: Na'im, "delightful, lovely," may describe the name of the LORD or the act of singing to it.
b: The Hebrew ki na'im can refer back to "his name" (so the Greek, "for it is lovely") or to the act of praise, as in 147:1: "Making music to our God is good; / it is sweet." The Plain English Translation keeps the ambiguity with "that is a delight."

a: Israel to be his own private treasure
p: Segullah is a king's own treasure, set apart from the state treasury. God calls Israel that at Sinai.
b: In 1 Chronicles 29:3 David gives his own segullah, his private store of gold and silver, for the temple. At Sinai God says: "out of all the peoples you will be my own private treasure. For the whole earth belongs to me" (Exodus 19:5). The word comes again in Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2; 26:18, and Malachi 3:17. 1 Peter 2:9 applies the Greek form of it ("a people for his own possession") to the church.
r: Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 14:2; 1 Chronicles 29:3; Malachi 3:17; 1 Peter 2:9

a: our Lord is above every god
p: The verse compares the LORD with other gods. Readers differ on what that says about the gods.
b: Some scholars hear an older stage of belief in which Israel's God was the greatest among many (compare 82:1; 86:8; 95:3). Others note that the same psalm calls the nations' gods mere idols, "something human hands have made" (135:15), and read "gods" as a way of speaking of rival powers or of what people worship. Jethro's confession is the model: "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods" (Exodus 18:11).

a: lets the wind out of his storerooms
p: Ancient poetry pictured storehouses in the sky for wind, snow and hail.
b: Job 38:22 speaks of "the storehouses of the snow" and "the storehouses of the hail." Canaanite poems give Baal the clouds, lightning and rain. Psalm 135:7 (repeated in Jeremiah 10:13; 51:16) gives all of it to the LORD: clouds rise at his word, lightning goes out with the rain, wind leaves his storerooms. The verdict: the psalm borrows common weather imagery to say that the storm god's tasks belong to Israel's God, who is not part of nature but its maker.

a: Sihon king of the Amorites
p: The first victories east of the Jordan were remembered in song and prayer for centuries.
b: Sihon ruled from Heshbon, north of the Arnon; Og ruled Bashan, the high plain east of the Sea of Galilee (Numbers 21:21–35; Deuteronomy 2:26–3:11). Their defeat was the first taste of the promised land, and both psalms 135 and 136 list them by name. Their story is repeated in Nehemiah 9:22 and Joshua 2:10. No inscription outside the Bible mentions either king.

a: For the LORD will judge his people
p: To "judge his people" here means to take their side: to give them justice.
b: The line is quoted from the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:36). Yadin, "he will judge," in this setting means "he will vindicate, plead their cause" (as in 54:1; Genesis 30:6), not condemn them. Codex Sinaiticus (first hand) has a different verb here ("he will have compassion"); the other Greek copies have "he will judge." Hebrews 10:30 quotes the line in its other sense, as a warning: "The Lord will judge his people."

a: The nations' idols are silver and gold
p: Verses 15–18 repeat Psalm 115:4–8 with small changes.
b: The idols have mouths, eyes and ears but cannot use them; their makers become like them. Psalm 135:17 adds "not even breath is in their mouths," where 115:7 had hands and feet. The Hebrew word for "breath" (ruach) also means "spirit": the idols have no life-giving spirit (Jeremiah 10:14; Habakkuk 2:19). See the notes on 115:4–8.

a: House of Levi, bless the LORD!
p: Psalm 115:9–11 named three groups; here a fourth, the house of Levi, is added.
b: Israel, the house of Aaron (the priests), the house of Levi (the temple Levites, a separate group after the exile, Ezra 6:16–20; Nehemiah 12), and "you who fear the LORD." Some take the last as converts from the nations who worshiped Israel's God, like the "God-fearers" of Acts 10:2; others as a summary of all the faithful. Rashi says they are the converts.

a: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good
p: Hodu is "give thanks" or "praise." The verb also means to confess or acknowledge.
b: Yadah (here hodu) means to praise by declaring what someone has done; the same verb is used of confessing sin (32:5). Its noun todah is a thank-offering (Leviticus 7:12). The opening line is Israel's oldest refrain, sung when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34), at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3), and when the foundation of the second temple was laid (Ezra 3:11). Jeremiah promised it would be heard again in the ruined city (Jeremiah 33:11).

a: for his loyal love is forever
p: Every one of the 26 verses ends with the same line: "his loyal love is forever."
b: Ki le'olam chasdo: "for to forever (is) his hesed." Hesed is the love that keeps faith within a covenant: steady, loyal, generous beyond duty. The KJV rendered it "mercy," and newer versions "steadfast love" or "faithful love"; the site uses "loyal love" throughout. The refrain seems to have been a response: a leader sang the first half of each verse and the people answered (compare 2 Chronicles 7:3, 6; Ezra 3:11). It turns history and creation into one long act of hesed.

a: for his loyal love is forever
p: 26 refrains in the Hebrew: the Talmud links them to 26 generations, later preachers to the name YHWH.
b: The Talmud links the 26 refrains to the 26 generations from Adam to Moses, when the world lived on God's hesed before the Torah was given (Bavli Pesachim 118a; Rashi). Later Jewish preachers often add that 26 is the number value of YHWH (Y = 10, H = 5, W = 6, H = 5). Whether the psalm was designed that way is doubtful: letters as numbers are first attested in Hebrew on coins of the Hasmonean period (100s–first century BC), and the count is not fixed in the witnesses. The Greek and the Gallican Latin have 27 refrains (see the variant on 136:26), and the Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 adds one in 136:8.

a: to him who does great wonders, he alone
p: Nifla'ot gedolot: deeds beyond human power. "He alone" stresses that no other god shares them.
b: Nifla'ot, "wonders," are God's mighty acts in creation and at the exodus (Exodus 3:20; Joshua 3:5; Psalm 72:18; Psalm 86:10). "He alone" (levaddo) answers the question of 135:5: the LORD has no partner. The Greek adds "alone" in 136:7 as well. The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a) lacks "great" in 136:4: "to him who does wonders, he alone."

a: to him who stretched the earth flat on top of the waters
p: The verse uses the ancient picture of the earth spread like a plate over the deep.
b: Roqa', "stretch out, beat flat," is the verb of raqia', "vault" (Genesis 1:6), used of hammering metal into sheets (Exodus 39:3). The earth is spread over the waters of the deep, as in 24:2. Babylonian myth told of Marduk splitting the body of the sea monster Tiamat to make the sky and the earth. The verdict: Israel shares the ancient picture of the world, but the psalm gives no battle and no monster: the LORD made it "with skill" (136:5), as an architect.

a: to him who struck Egypt in its firstborn
p: Verses 4–9 tell of creation; verses 10–22 of the exodus and the land. The same God did both.
b: The psalm moves straight from the sun, moon and stars to the death of Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:29). The Creator who set lights "to govern" is also the one who overthrows Pharaoh's rule. The same order of creation followed by history shapes Nehemiah's great prayer (Nehemiah 9:6–25) and the Passover service.

a: to him who cut the Sea of Reeds into pieces
p: Gazar means to cut, and its noun gezarim means pieces, the word used of the animals split at the covenant with Abraham.
b: Only here is the dividing of the sea described with gazar and gezarim, "pieces." The same noun names the halves of animals between which God passed in his covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15:17, gezarim). Rashi, following older Jewish tradition, says "into pieces" means twelve, one path for each tribe. On the name "Sea of Reeds" (Yam Suf), see Exodus 13:18.

a: and shook Pharaoh and his army off into the Sea of Reeds
p: Na'ar means to shake off, as one shakes dust from a garment. It is the word used in Exodus 14:27.
b: "The LORD shook Egypt off into the middle of the sea" (Exodus 14:27). The verb is used of shaking dust off (Isaiah 52:2) or shaking out a fold of cloth (Nehemiah 5:13). Pharaoh's army is no more to God than dust on a sleeve.

a: who remembered us when we were brought low
p: The last verses move from "Israel" to "us": the singers' own rescue, perhaps from Babylon.
b: Shiflenu, "our lowness," is the humiliation of defeat (Ecclesiastes 10:6). After the land is given (136:21–22), the psalm adds a later rescue: God "tore us free from our foes." Many think this is the return from exile, so that the singers set their own story in line with the exodus. Mary's song uses the same idea: he "has looked with care on the lowliness of his slave" (Luke 1:48).

a: who gives food to every living thing
p: The Talmud calls this psalm the Great Hallel because God sits on high and gives food to every creature.
b: Rabbi Yochanan explains the name: "Because the Holy One, blessed be He, sits in the heights of the world and distributes food to every creature" (Bavli Pesachim 118a). Opinions differ there on how far the Great Hallel reaches: Psalm 136 alone, or from 135:4 or from Psalm 134 to the end of 136. The "Egyptian Hallel" is Psalms 113–118. Jews recite Psalm 136 in the Sabbath and festival morning service and at the Passover seder.

a: Give thanks to the God of the heavens
p: "God of the heavens" is the title used for Israel's God in the Persian period.
b: El hashamayim appears only here in the Psalms. The phrase "God of the heavens" is common in Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel (Ezra 1:2; Nehemiah 1:4; Daniel 2:18), and in the Aramaic letters from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt (about 410 BC). It suits a psalm sung after the exile. Most Greek copies and the Gallican Latin add one more line: "Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever" (see the variant).

a: Beside the rivers of Babylon
p: Babylonia was laced with canals off the Euphrates and Tigris. Judean exiles were settled along them.
b: Ezekiel lived among the exiles "by the Chebar canal" (Ezekiel 1:1, 3; 3:15). Cuneiform tablets from Al-Yahudu, "Judah-town," a village of Judean exiles near Nippur, record their business from about 572 to 477 BC: they farmed, paid taxes and gave their children Hebrew names (Pearce and Wunsch 2014). Exiles were not slaves in chains but uprooted people far from home. "Sat" is the posture of mourning (Job 2:13; Ezra 9:3; Nehemiah 1:4).

a: On the poplar trees in that land
p: The KJV has "willows." The tree is probably the Euphrates poplar.
b: 'Aravim are the trees of streams (Isaiah 44:4; Leviticus 23:40). In Mesopotamia this is most likely the Euphrates poplar (Populus euphratica). The older English "willows" led Linnaeus in 1753 to name the weeping willow Salix babylonica, though that tree comes from China. Rashi glosses them "willows of the brook."

a: "Sing for us from Zion's songs!"
p: The captors may be mocking, or simply curious. Either way, the exiles refuse.
b: "Songs of Zion" may be the psalms of the temple, such as 46, 48, 76 and 87, which praise the city that "will not totter" (46:5). To sing them on demand, beside ruins, would be bitter. Tolalenu, "our tormentors," is a rare word, perhaps "those who heaped us in ruins" (the Greek reads "those who led us away," the Targum "our plunderers"; Rashi suggests either mockers or musical instruments). In 1800s America, enslaved Africans and their descendants sang Psalm 137 as their own lament, and Frederick Douglass quoted it in his Fourth of July speech of 1852.

What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?

a: How can we sing the LORD's song
p: The question is not whether God can hear in Babylon, but whether temple song belongs on foreign soil.
b: Foreign land was thought unclean (Amos 7:17; Hosea 9:3–4); sacrifice could be offered only in the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:5–14). Yet Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7), and Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem three times a day (Daniel 6:10). Synagogue prayer grew partly out of this question. The Psalter itself answers it: Psalm 137 is a song of Zion sung in exile.
r: Amos 7:17; Hosea 9:3–4; Jeremiah 29:7; Daniel 6:10; 1 Kings 8:46–50; John 4:21–24

a: let my right hand forget
p: The Hebrew says only "let my right hand forget," with no object. Many suggest a slightly different word, "wither."
b: "Let my right hand forget" leaves the reader to supply: forget its skill on the lyre. The Greek and Latin read a passive, "let my right hand be forgotten." Many scholars move one letter and read tikhchash or tikhsh, "let it grow numb, wither" (compare 109:24), which pairs well with "my tongue cling to my palate" in 137:6: a harpist who loses hand and voice. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; see the variant.

a: above the best of my joys
p: Jews remember Jerusalem in the middle of joy: at weddings, at meals, in the house itself.
b: The Talmud says that after the temple's destruction one may plaster a house but leave a small square bare, in memory, and that "the best of my joys" means the ashes placed on a bridegroom's head (Bavli Bava Batra 60b, citing these verses). Many Jewish weddings today recite 137:5–6 before the groom breaks a glass. On weekdays Psalm 137 is said before the grace after meals, while Psalm 126 is said on Sabbaths and feasts.

a: against the people of Edom
t: Edom on the day of Jerusalem
p: When Babylon took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the Edomites, Judah's neighbors and kin, joined in.
b: Edom descended from Esau, Jacob's brother (Genesis 36:1). Obadiah accuses Edom of standing by, looting and cutting off fugitives "on the day of their calamity" (Obadiah 10–14). Lamentations 4:21–22 and Ezekiel 25:12–14; 35:5 say the same, and 1 Esdras 4:45 claims the Edomites burned the temple, in Codex Alexandrinus and the KJV (Codex Vaticanus reads "the Jews"). The betrayal by a brother nation hurt as much as the conquest. In later Jewish reading, Edom became a name for Rome, the destroyer of the second temple.
r: Obadiah 10–14; Lamentations 4:21–22; Ezekiel 25:12–14; Ezekiel 35:5; Joel 3:19; 1 Esdras 4:45

a: "Tear it bare! Tear it bare
p: 'Aru, 'aru: "strip it, strip it." The verb is used of emptying a jar and of stripping a body.
b: 'Arah means "lay bare, empty out" (Genesis 24:20, of emptying a jar; Isaiah 3:17; Habakkuk 3:13, "laying bare the foundation"). The doubled shout echoes the mob. "Right down to the foundation in it" means level the city to bedrock. The Greek renders it "Empty it, empty it."
orig: עָרוּ עָרוּ עַד הַיְסוֹד בָּהּ ('aru 'aru 'ad haysod bah)

a: Daughter Babylon, you who will be laid waste
p: The Hebrew says "the one devastated" or "to be devastated." Many versions change it to "destroyer."
b: Hashedudah is a passive form: "the one laid waste," or (looking ahead) "doomed to destruction." Some scholars and translations read an active form, "destroyer." The Greek has hē talaipōros, "wretched," and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew vastata, "laid waste." Babylon was taken by Cyrus in 539 BC without being destroyed; its long decline came later. The prophets foresaw its fall (Isaiah 13; Jeremiah 50–51).

a: happy is the one who pays you back
p: The cry asks for justice by the law of like for like: what Babylon did, let it suffer.
b: Ashrei, "happy," is the word that opens Psalm 1. Here it blesses the one who repays Babylon. The demand is the law of retaliation (Exodus 21:23–25), which limits punishment to what was done. Jeremiah says the same: "Repay her by her own works; whatever she did, do it to her" (Jeremiah 50:29, fresh rendering), and Revelation takes it up of the last Babylon: "Repay her as she herself has repaid" (Revelation 18:6).

a: and shatters them on the rock
p: Killing a conquered city's children was a known horror of ancient war. Jerusalem's children had suffered it.
b: The Old Testament speaks of it in several places: Elisha weeps that Hazael will "smash their little ones" (2 Kings 8:12); Hosea 13:16, Nahum 3:10 and Isaiah 13:16 (of Babylon itself) say the same. Lamentations 2:20 and 4:10 describe the fate of Jerusalem's children in the siege. The speaker asks that Babylon suffer what it did, and the cry ends the psalm without comment. "The rock" (hassela') may also point to Sela, Edom's rock fortress (2 Kings 14:7). See the chapter page for how the traditions read and pray it.
r: 2 Kings 8:12; Hosea 13:16; Nahum 3:10; Isaiah 13:16; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10

a: Happy is the one who grabs your babies
p: Four main answers: an honest cry left to God, a prophecy, an allegory, or words not to be prayed.
b: (1) An honest cry: the psalm hands vengeance to God, rather than taking it (Romans 12:19); Zenger and Brueggemann read it so, as the prayer of victims. (2) Prophecy: Calvin heard the Spirit announcing Babylon's judgment, as in Isaiah 13:16. (3) Allegory: Augustine and Benedict read "babies" as sinful thoughts at their birth, and "the rock" as Christ. (4) Not for Christian prayer: the Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves out verses 7–9. C. S. Lewis wrote that the curses show what injustice does to its victims, and that it is wrong to pretend otherwise.
